title: Contract-manufacturing sourcing broker for CNC machining & sheet-metal parts (Midwest job-shop network)
product_service: Build-to-print custom parts and small assemblies (CNC machined, laser/sheet metal, weldments, with outside finishing) sourced from vetted independent job shops. Broker quotes, takes the PO and title, manages the supplier, inspects, and delivers.
target_customer: Design/manufacturing engineers and buyers at small-to-mid OEMs, machine builders, R&D labs and hardware startups (10-500 employees) needing prototypes and low-volume production. Illinois alone has 4,371 manufacturing establishments with 20+ employees [C, WS03-S006].
purchase_motivation: Speed and one point of contact; shortage of vetted shop capacity; avoiding supplier vetting; DFM help; domestic/USMCA sourcing to manage 2025-26 tariffs.
spending_evidence: Xometry marketplace revenue $629.6M in FY2025 from 81,821 active buyers (~$7.7k marketplace revenue per buyer, analyst calc) [B, WS03-S001]; Protolabs network (outsourced) revenue $116.2M, +15.7% [B, WS03-S002]; US machine shops shipped $44.7B in 2022 [C, WS03-S007].
representative_operators: Xometry - $686.6M revenue FY2025, marketplace GM 34.7%, still GAAP loss-making (net loss $61.7M) [B, WS03-S001]
Protolabs network segment - $116.2M FY2025 [B, WS03-S002]
Fictiv - ~250 partner factories, sold to MISUMI for $350M in 2025 after three loss years [C, WS03-S004; D, WS03-S005]
Independent human-led sourcing brokers - count and economics MISSING [E]
revenue_mechanism: Markup on supplier cost: customer price minus supplier price, finishing and freight. Incumbent platform realizes 34.7% marketplace gross margin [B, WS03-S001]; a new entrant competing on price is assumed 15-30% [E].
typical_transaction_value: $500-$15,000 per prototype PO; approved production programs $5k-$100k+/yr per part family [E]
direct_costs: Supplier part cost, outside processing (plating, heat treat, anodize), freight, inspection labor, rework/remake credits, card fees.
contribution_profit_note: Example: $5,000 PO at 22% gross margin = ~$1,100 gross profit before founder time and overhead [E]. Platform benchmark: $218.3M marketplace gross profit / 81,821 buyers = ~$2.7k gross profit per active buyer per year [B-derived, WS03-S001].
working_capital_note: Customers (OEMs) commonly pay net-30 to net-60; new suppliers may require prepayment or net-30. The broker can be funding 30-60 days of COGS, roughly 10-20% of annual revenue at scale [E]. Remakes after quality escapes are absorbed by the broker.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks from first RFQ to prototype PO; 3-12 months to win production programs (first-article, supplier approval).
repeat_purchase: recurring-programs: approved production parts reorder; prototypes episodic
acquisition_channels: Direct outreach to engineering/purchasing at Midwest OEMs identified via CBP/NAICS and directories
SEO RFQ landing pages by process/material
Referrals from job shops turning away out-of-scope work
Industrial trade shows and local manufacturing associations
customer_accessibility: Buyers are identifiable and reachable by B2B outreach. Many already use instant-quote platforms or trusted shops. Switching is easy for prototypes and slow for production parts.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed, not confirmed. Illinois has 829 machine shops and 182 sheet-metal shops [C, WS03-S006], and many are small (SUSB: 9,786 US machine-shop firms under $1M receipts [C, WS03-S008]) and lack sales staff. Xometry's 4,996 active suppliers show shops accept intermediaries [B, WS03-S001]. Willingness to quote a new broker reliably is unverified.
competitive_intensity: high - Xometry, Protolabs network, Fictiv/MISUMI, Chinese platforms, plus direct relationships with shops
entry_strategy: A human, engineer-led service for work that instant-quote engines handle poorly: complex tight-tolerance or multi-process parts, kitted assemblies, and drawings needing DFM. Offer a site-audited Chicago/Rockford supply base and documented domestic/USMCA origin for buyers who are tariff- or ITAR-sensitive. Quote within 24 hours.
licenses: Illinois business registration and IDOR sales-tax registration/resale certificates; general and product liability insurance; ITAR (DDTC) registration only if handling defense articles, which should be avoided initially [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low. Quality-system expectations (ISO 9001/AS9100) for aerospace and medical buyers; export controls (ITAR/EAR) for defense-related drawings.
operational_risks: Supplier late deliveries and quality escapes for which the broker is liable; disintermediation (customer goes direct to the shop); drawing confidentiality; founder quoting errors.
financial_risks: Receivables concentration with a few OEMs; funding remakes; supplier prepayment for new accounts.
geographic_constraints: Customers can be nationwide. Supplier audits favor a local supply base, and Chicago metro + Rockford hold most Illinois machine shops (Cook 222, DuPage 116, Winnebago 90) [C, WS03-S006].
founder_expertise: Blueprint/GD&T reading, machining and fabrication process knowledge, cost estimating, supplier auditing, first-article inspection basics.
staffing: Solo in year 1. Year 2: a quoting/project manager and a QC inspector (market wages, roughly $55-80k each [E]). Later: account managers, each owning a book of buyers.
automation_potential: AI and software can parse drawings, package RFQs, match suppliers, compare quotes, chase follow-ups and draft DFM notes. Supplier relationships, negotiation, quality judgement and dispute handling stay human.
delegation_potential: Medium. Account-manager and buyer roles exist in the labor market. Early supplier trust is tied to the founder.
scalability: Scales with account managers and supplier depth. Each account manager may carry roughly $250-500k gross profit per year at maturity [E]. More processes can be added (molding, castings).
expansion: Add injection molding (WS03-003) and reverse engineering (WS03-030). Then vertically integrate inspection, finishing (WS03-028) or a small CNC cell (WS03-026) only for proven repeat parts. Add private-label standard components.
roic_note: Capital at risk is mainly working capital ($10-50k) plus small tooling and insurance. If receivables are controlled, operating profit / capital can exceed 200% [E].
critical_assumptions: A new broker can win RFQs against instant-quote platforms at 15-30% markup
Local shops will quote reliably and hold quality for a broker
Buyers accept a broker without ISO 9001 initially
unanswered_questions: Realized markups of small independent brokers
Share of Illinois shops willing to work through a broker
Disintermediation rate after year 1
Typical supplier payment terms for a new broker
failure_modes: One quality escape loses a key account
Customers or suppliers cut out the broker
Founder remains the only salesperson and quoter
score_rationale: roic 8: near-zero fixed capital, with public comps showing intermediaries keep ~35% gross margin. entry 4: crowded with well-funded platforms; the wedge is service and complexity. fcf 5: plausible $100-150k by year 3-5 with 1-2 staff. cash 4: the broker carries net-30/60 receivables against supplier terms.
preliminary_verdict: advance - lowest-capital entry into manufacturing; public comps prove buyers pay ~35% gross margin to intermediaries; needs a defensible complexity/local wedge.

title: Tariff-driven reshoring/nearshoring sourcing agent for importers (US & Mexico supplier transition)
product_service: Supplier search, RFQs, landed-cost and tariff comparison, supplier qualification (FAI/PPAP), and transition management for importers moving castings, forgings, machined, molded or fabricated components from Asia to US or USMCA-qualifying Mexican suppliers. Paid as a project fee plus success fee, or as ongoing broker margin.
target_customer: Purchasing/supply-chain managers at small-to-mid US importers and OEMs ($10-300M revenue) buying imported components.
purchase_motivation: Section 301 duties of generally 10-12.5% on 60 partners effective Jul 24, 2026 [C, WS03-S010]; 50% Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper [C, WS03-S011]; USMCA-qualifying goods excluded [C, WS03-S010]; policy volatility after IEEPA tariffs were struck down [C, WS03-S009, WS03-S033].
spending_evidence: Indirect only: trade press reports Protolabs network margins hurt by tariff inefficiencies [C, WS03-S003]. Fees actually paid for reshoring sourcing services are MISSING.
representative_operators: Xometry/Fictiv offer domestic and offshore networks [B, WS03-S001; C, WS03-S004]
Independent reshoring consultants and sourcing agents - names and economics MISSING [E]
revenue_mechanism: Project fee $5-25k plus a success fee of 3-5% of first-year spend, or conversion to broker markup [E].
typical_transaction_value: $5,000-$25,000 project; success fees on $100k-$2M annual spend [E]
direct_costs: Founder/analyst time, travel to supplier sites (incl. Mexico), sample and inspection costs, tariff-classification advisory (licensed customs broker if needed).
contribution_profit_note: One $15k project at ~70% gross margin = ~$10k contribution [E].
working_capital_note: Retainers can be billed upfront. Success fees lag 3-12 months behind supplier transition.
sales_cycle: 2-6 months; decisions stall when tariff rulings are pending (Section 301 litigation at CIT [C, WS03-S010]).
repeat_purchase: occasional - project-based; can convert to recurring broker margin
acquisition_channels: Outreach to importers identifiable through public import records
Referrals from customs brokers and freight forwarders
customer_accessibility: Importers are identifiable, but credibility walls are high and the deciders are busy. Many will run the exercise in-house or with existing suppliers.
supplier_accessibility: US job shops reachable (see WS03-001). Mexican suppliers require travel and network building. Unconfirmed.
competitive_intensity: moderate - consultancies, freight forwarders, platforms, and OEMs' own purchasing
entry_strategy: Narrow on one commodity (e.g., machined aluminum or castings) and buyers in one region. Publish transparent landed-cost comparisons, then take execution risk by acting as broker.
licenses: None for sourcing advice. Customs brokerage (filing entries for others) requires a CBP customs broker license, so it must be referred out [E].
regulatory_barriers: Must avoid acting as an unlicensed customs broker; country-of-origin/USMCA rules-of-origin accuracy.
operational_risks: Tariff reversals erase the savings case mid-project; supplier transitions fail at first article.
financial_risks: Success fees uncollectable if customer reverses; demand collapses if tariffs fall.
geographic_constraints: National market; Mexico travel needed for nearshoring.
founder_expertise: Tariff/HTS basics, rules of origin, manufacturing process costing, supplier qualification.
staffing: Solo initially; later analysts. Execution staff overlap with WS03-001.
automation_potential: AI helps with landed-cost models, HTS research drafts, supplier discovery and RFQ packaging. Judgement, travel and negotiation stay human.
scalability: Limited as a standalone advisory business; scale comes from converting clients into WS03-001 broker revenue.
expansion: Feeds WS03-001/003. Possible Mexico supplier network as a moat.
roic_note: Capital trivial; returns depend on founder hours rather than capital [E].
critical_assumptions: Tariff differentials persist long enough to justify supplier switches
Importers pay outsiders rather than doing it in-house
unanswered_questions: What fees/success fees buyers actually pay
Durability of Section 301 duties after CIT litigation
Mexico supplier accessibility for a newcomer
failure_modes: Policy whiplash makes the savings case vanish
Clients take the supplier list and execute themselves
score_rationale: resilience 3: demand is created by litigated, volatile tariff policy. access 4: credibility wall with importers. roic 8: almost no capital. Best used as a wedge into WS03-001 rather than as a standalone business.
preliminary_verdict: hold - real but policy-volatile demand; use as a marketing wedge for WS03-001 rather than a standalone business.

title: Injection molding & mold-tooling sourcing broker (domestic + nearshore molders)
product_service: Plastic injection-molded parts plus the molds that make them. The broker runs DFM, the tooling build, T1 sample approval and production runs at partner molders, and owns customer communication.
target_customer: Product companies, OEMs and hardware startups needing 1k-500k molded parts/yr.
purchase_motivation: Molding and tooling expertise is scarce; molders' minimums and gatekeeping; tariffs on imported molded parts and molds [C, WS03-S010].
spending_evidence: US 'all other plastics products' (326199) shipments $122.7B in 2022; Illinois 356 establishments, $7.2B [C, WS03-S007]. Protolabs injection molding revenue fell 1.4% in 2025 [C, WS03-S003].
representative_operators: Protolabs (owned molding + network) [B, WS03-S002]
Xometry and Fictiv networks include molding [B, WS03-S001; C, WS03-S004]
Independent tooling brokers - MISSING
revenue_mechanism: Margin on tooling (10-25%) plus markup on production parts (15-30%) [E].
direct_costs: Mold build, molder part price, resin surcharges, samples, freight/duties, inspection.
contribution_profit_note: $30k mold at 15% = $4.5k, plus $50k/yr parts at 20% = $10k/yr recurring gross profit per program [E].
working_capital_note: Industry practice of tooling deposits (often ~50% upfront [E]) funds mold builds. Production parts are net-30/60 against molder terms.
sales_cycle: 2-6 months to award a mold; 8-16 weeks to T1 samples [E].
repeat_purchase: recurring-programs: production reorders for life of the product
acquisition_channels: Outreach to product companies and engineering firms
customer_accessibility: Reachable, but each program is a considered purchase with long gestation.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: Illinois has 620 plastics/rubber establishments [C, WS03-S006]; molder willingness to work with a broker unverified.
competitive_intensity: high - platforms, Asian tooling houses, direct molders
entry_strategy: Own the 'tooling transition' niche: move molds from China to US/Mexico molders, or re-source orphaned molds; DFM-heavy service.
licenses: Business/sales-tax registration; product liability insurance [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low; medical/food-contact parts need certified molders (FDA/ISO 13485).
operational_risks: Tool defects, slips at T1, resin shortages; disputes over mold ownership.
financial_risks: Mold rework costs; customer cancels after tooling started.
founder_expertise: Plastics part design, mold design basics, resin selection, PPAP.
staffing: Solo, then a project engineer with molding background.
automation_potential: AI-assisted DFM checks, RFQ packaging and quote comparison. Tooling judgement stays human.
scalability: Programs accumulate recurring part revenue; scales with project engineers.
expansion: Combine with WS03-001; private-label molded products.
roic_note: Asset-light; tooling deposits reduce capital need [E].
critical_assumptions: Customers pay tooling deposits upfront
Molders accept brokered programs
unanswered_questions: Typical broker margins on molds vs parts
Molder capacity/attitude in Illinois
failure_modes: Customers move production direct to molder after tooling
score_rationale: cash 6: tooling deposits help. access 4: few, slow, considered purchases. Otherwise similar to WS03-001 but with longer cycles and higher technical risk.
preliminary_verdict: hold - add as a second process line once WS03-001 has a customer base.

title: PCBA & cable/wire-harness contract-manufacturing broker
product_service: Brokered printed-circuit-board assembly and cable/wire-harness builds from partner EMS shops, including component sourcing (turnkey) or consigned kits.
target_customer: Electronics OEMs, instrumentation makers and startups with low-to-mid volumes.
purchase_motivation: Small-volume EMS capacity is hard to get; component sourcing burden; tariffs on Asian PCBA [C, WS03-S010].
spending_evidence: US PCBA (334418) shipments $24.5B in 2022 with materials 71.4% of shipments; Illinois 47 establishments, $1.05B [C, WS03-S007].
representative_operators: Domestic EMS shops (47 in IL) [C, WS03-S007]
Asian online PCBA services - economics MISSING
revenue_mechanism: Markup on EMS quote and components (8-20%) [E].
direct_costs: EMS assembly price, components (often >70% of value), test fixtures, freight.
contribution_profit_note: Census shows PCBA residual after materials, payroll, benefits, services, depreciation and rent of only ~5.0% of shipments for the makers themselves [C, WS03-S007]. Broker margin sits on a thin base.
working_capital_note: Turnkey builds require buying components (often prepaid, sometimes with long lead times), creating heavy working capital and obsolescence risk.
sales_cycle: 1-4 months; qualification for production.
customer_accessibility: Moderate; engineers are reachable but price-sensitive and used to online Asian quotes.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed; 47 IL PCBA shops [C, WS03-S007].
competitive_intensity: extreme - online Asian PCBA services, domestic EMS direct sales
entry_strategy: Domestic quick-turn for regulated or ITAR-adjacent buyers; harness/cable builds where Asian lead times hurt.
licenses: Business registration; ITAR only if defense (avoid) [E].
operational_risks: Component counterfeits, shortages, test escapes.
automation_potential: BOM scrubbing, component availability search, quote comparison.
expansion: Box-build, harnesses for machine builders.
roic_note: Working capital in components drags ROIC [E].
critical_assumptions: Buyers pay a premium for domestic quick-turn
unanswered_questions: Broker margins realized in EMS
Component sourcing terms available to a newcomer
failure_modes: Thin margins wiped by a single bad build
score_rationale: Census shows materials are 71% of PCBA value with ~5% residual for makers, so broker margins are thin. cash 3: components prepaid. entry 3: online Asian services dominate.
preliminary_verdict: reject - thin margin base and component working-capital risk; inferior to mechanical-parts brokerage (WS03-001).

title: Obsolete & surplus industrial-automation parts reseller (tested inventory: PLCs, drives, servos)
subindustry: Surplus/obsolete automation and MRO parts resale
product_service: New-surplus and used/tested PLCs, VFDs, HMIs, servo motors/drives, sensors and fluid-power components from discontinued or long-lead lines. Sold with test reports and a warranty via eBay, an own site and directly to plant maintenance departments.
target_customer: Maintenance managers and reliability engineers at plants running legacy equipment; machine builders supporting old installs; other resellers.
purchase_motivation: Downtime cost when an obsolete part fails; OEM discontinued lines; new-part lead times; repair vs replace economics.
spending_evidence: Radwell has built a large private business on new, surplus and reconditioned automation parts (third-party revenue estimates conflict: $231M vs $350M) [D, WS03-S023]. eBay PLC listings show active sales (e.g., one sealed Allen-Bradley unit with 102 sold) [D, WS03-S025]. Price gap used ~$2.5-4k vs refurbished $6k+ for the same part (vendor claim) [D, WS03-S024].
representative_operators: Radwell International - private, multi-site, repair center in NJ [D, WS03-S023]
NJT Automation - surplus/refurb supplier [D, WS03-S024]
Many small eBay Business & Industrial sellers - count MISSING [D]
revenue_mechanism: Buy surplus lots from plant closures, auctions and excess-inventory buyouts, test, and resell item by item. eBay final value fee 13.6% up to $7,500 per item for most Business & Industrial categories [B, WS03-S020].
direct_costs: Lot purchase cost, testing labor/bench, marketplace fees (13.6%) [B, WS03-S020], shipping/packaging, returns/warranty, storage.
contribution_profit_note: Example: $800 sale of a part bought within a $40-150 lot allocation, minus ~$110 eBay fee and $30 shipping = ~$500+ contribution [E]. Slow-moving long tail dilutes the average.
working_capital_note: Inventory-heavy. Lots are paid for at auction and sold over months to years. Sales are paid at order via marketplace, so receivables are negligible. Dead stock is the main trap.
sales_cycle: Marketplace: immediate; direct B2B: quote-to-PO in days for urgent breakdowns.
repeat_purchase: occasional per buyer; continuous marketplace demand; plant accounts reorder
acquisition_channels: Own SEO catalog site with part-number pages
Direct to Midwest plant maintenance departments
customer_accessibility: Buyers actively search by part number in a breakdown, which is one of the few industrial niches with inbound search demand [D].
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: auctions, plant closures, distributor excess, and customers' own surplus. Competition for good lots from established surplus dealers. Illinois' 12,465 manufacturing establishments are a large regional source [C, WS03-S006].
competitive_intensity: high - Radwell, large surplus houses, many eBay sellers, grey-market/counterfeit sellers
entry_strategy: Specialize in one brand family (e.g., legacy Allen-Bradley/Fanuc). Test every unit on a bench and ship with a 1-year warranty and same-day dispatch. Offer Chicago-area local pickup and buy customers' surplus for credit.
licenses: Illinois business and sales-tax registration; no special license. Must describe 'new surplus' accurately (no OEM warranty) to avoid trademark/consumer-protection exposure [E].
regulatory_barriers: Counterfeit risk; OEM objections to 'authorized' claims; export controls for some drives to certain countries.
operational_risks: Mis-tested items; counterfeit inventory; storage sprawl; marketplace account suspension.
geographic_constraints: None for sales; sourcing benefits from Midwest plant density.
founder_expertise: Automation hardware identification, test procedures, pricing research, marketplace operations.
staffing: Part-time lister/shipper by month 6; bench test tech by year 2.
automation_potential: AI can identify parts from nameplate photos, generate listings, research comparable sales and pricing, and keep the catalog. Testing, sourcing negotiation and lot valuation stay human.
delegation_potential: Good - listing, shipping and testing are standard roles.
scalability: Constrained by sourcing of good lots and capital; small sellers plateau at roughly $1-5M revenue [E].
expansion: Add component repair (WS03-020), sourcing service (WS03-006), and reverse engineering (WS03-030).
roic_note: Inventory turns drive ROIC. If $50k inventory turns 1.5x at 45% margin, ~$34k gross profit per turn-year on $50k (~70%) before overhead [E].
critical_assumptions: Good lots can be bought at a fraction of resale value
Testing capability can be built for the chosen brand family
unanswered_questions: Realized sell-through rates for surplus automation inventory
Auction prices for surplus lots in the Midwest
Counterfeit prevalence in the chosen category
failure_modes: Counterfeit or failed units destroy marketplace reputation
Big surplus houses outbid for lots
score_rationale: access 7: buyers search by part number in urgent breakdowns. cash 4: inventory-heavy. fcf 4: typical small seller earnings modest. ai 6: listing/catalog automation is a real cost lever.
preliminary_verdict: advance - fast first revenue with inbound demand and strong synergies with repair and sourcing; main risks are inventory discipline and counterfeits.

title: Hard-to-find & obsolete MRO part sourcing service (no inventory, back-to-back buying for plant maintenance)
product_service: Rapid sourcing of discontinued or long-lead mechanical, electrical and automation parts for plant maintenance. Search broker and surplus networks, verify authenticity and condition, buy back-to-back against the customer PO, and ship with a warranty.
target_customer: Maintenance/purchasing at mid-size plants (50-500 employees); Illinois has 2,329 manufacturing establishments with 50+ employees [C, WS03-S006].
purchase_motivation: Line-down urgency; internal buyers lack time and surplus-market know-how.
spending_evidence: Indirect: Radwell's business of sourcing obsolete parts [D, WS03-S023]; surplus price dispersion [D, WS03-S024]. Direct evidence of sourcing-service fees MISSING.
representative_operators: Radwell (sourcing service as part of model) [D, WS03-S023]
Independent MRO sourcing brokers - MISSING
revenue_mechanism: Markup on parts bought back-to-back (20-35%) plus expedite fees [E].
direct_costs: Part cost, expedited freight, testing, returns.
contribution_profit_note: $2,000 part at 25% = $500 per sourced request [E].
working_capital_note: Buy only after customer PO; card payments for small orders; net-30 for accounts, so receivables are modest.
sales_cycle: Days per request; 1-3 months to become an approved vendor.
repeat_purchase: occasional-recurring: breakdown-driven, frequent at multi-line plants
acquisition_channels: Part-number SEO pages that capture inbound requests
customer_accessibility: Maintenance managers are reachable; getting on approved-vendor lists takes persistence.
supplier_accessibility: Broker/surplus networks exist; quality varies (counterfeit risk).
competitive_intensity: moderate - surplus houses, distributors' own sourcing desks
entry_strategy: 'Line-down desk' with a 4-hour response promise, verified-authenticity reports and no-find/no-fee.
licenses: Business/sales-tax registration [E].
operational_risks: Counterfeit parts; failure to find; returns.
financial_risks: Low; back-to-back purchasing limits inventory risk.
automation_potential: AI for cross-referencing part numbers, finding alternates, searching listings and drafting quotes. Verification stays human.
scalability: Scales with sourcing specialists; becomes an MRO account relationship.
expansion: Feeds WS03-005 inventory, WS03-020 repair, WS03-030 reverse engineering, WS03-010 VMI.
roic_note: Minimal capital; ROIC driven by founder/staff time [E].
critical_assumptions: Plants pay 20-35% markups for sourcing speed
unanswered_questions: Request volume per plant per year
Approved-vendor onboarding friction
score_rationale: roic 8: no inventory. access 5: vendor-list friction. Best combined with WS03-005.
preliminary_verdict: advance (combined with WS03-005) - near-zero-capital way into plant maintenance budgets.

title: Surplus industrial equipment buy/refurbish/resell (used machine tools, packaging & process machinery)
product_service: Buy used CNC/fabrication machines and packaging/process equipment from closures, auctions and upgrades. Clean, test and lightly refurbish, then resell via online machinery marketplaces, eBay heavy-equipment categories and dealer networks.
target_customer: Job shops and small manufacturers buying used capacity; exporters; dealers.
purchase_motivation: Used equipment costs a fraction of new and is available immediately; tariff and possible Section 232 machinery duties raise new prices [C, WS03-S011].
spending_evidence: Liquidity Services FY2026 GMV $1.6B, with consignment 86% of Q4 GMV, and its Capital Assets Group (industrial surplus) Q3 GMV $57.5M [B, WS03-S022].
representative_operators: Liquidity Services platforms (consignment-led) [B, WS03-S022]
Regional used-machinery dealers - economics MISSING
revenue_mechanism: Spread between purchase (auction/closure) and resale price [E].
direct_costs: Purchase price, rigging/transport, storage, refurbishment parts, marketplace fees (eBay heavy equipment 3% to $15k [B, WS03-S020]).
contribution_profit_note: $40k machine bought at $25k, $6k rigging/refurb = ~$9k contribution [E].
working_capital_note: Heavy: purchased inventory held 1-6 months, plus storage and rigging costs. Buyers pay before pickup.
sales_cycle: Weeks to months per machine.
customer_accessibility: Buyers search actively for specific machines; trust in condition is the barrier.
supplier_accessibility: Auctions open to anyone; competition from established dealers; closures increase in downturns.
competitive_intensity: high - established dealers with rigging crews and warehouses
entry_strategy: Specialize in one class (e.g., Haas VMCs or packaging machines) with documented test runs and video.
licenses: Business/sales-tax registration; rigging insurance [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low; export controls for some machine tools.
operational_risks: Hidden defects; rigging damage/injury; storage.
financial_risks: Capital tied in large items; price declines in recessions.
automation_potential: Valuation comparables, listing creation. Physical work stays human.
expansion: Consignment (WS03-008), parts harvesting (WS03-005), rebuild/retrofit.
roic_note: Capital-intensive per deal; ROIC depends on turns [E].
critical_assumptions: Can buy below resale after rigging costs
Storage space affordable
unanswered_questions: Typical dealer spreads on used CNC
Midwest auction clearance prices
score_rationale: cash 3 and roic 4: capital tied in large items. delegation 4: valuation judgement is founder-centric.
preliminary_verdict: hold - capital-heavy trading on judgement margins; pursue only opportunistically alongside WS03-008.

title: Used-machinery consignment & plant-surplus brokerage (commission, no ownership)
product_service: List and sell manufacturers' surplus or upgraded equipment and plant contents on commission: valuation, photos/video, marketing, buyer qualification, inspection scheduling and rigging coordination. Small closures can be run as online auctions through partner platforms.
target_customer: Plant managers/CFOs at manufacturers upgrading, consolidating or closing; Illinois 12,465 manufacturing establishments [C, WS03-S006].
purchase_motivation: Recover cash from idle assets; clear floor space; avoid hassle.
spending_evidence: Liquidity Services' consignment model: 86% of Q4 FY2026 GMV on consignment; GovDeals revenue ~9.8% of GMV (analyst calc) [B, WS03-S022].
representative_operators: Liquidity Services (GovDeals, AllSurplus, CAG) [B, WS03-S022]
Regional auctioneers and brokers - MISSING
revenue_mechanism: Commission 5-15% of sale price or buyer's premium [E]; platform take rate benchmark ~10% [B-derived, WS03-S022].
direct_costs: Marketing/listing fees, photography, travel, platform fees.
contribution_profit_note: $50k machine at 10% = $5k per deal [E].
working_capital_note: Buyer pays before removal; commission deducted at settlement - positive cash flow.
sales_cycle: 1-3 months to win listing; 1-3 months to sell.
acquisition_channels: Referrals from accountants, bankers, lenders and turnaround advisors
customer_accessibility: Sellers exist but events (upgrades, closures) are sporadic and established auctioneers have relationships.
supplier_accessibility: N/A (sellers are the supply).
competitive_intensity: moderate-high - auction houses, dealers, platforms
entry_strategy: Small-lot specialist with faster turnaround and lower minimums than national auctioneers.
licenses: Illinois auctioneer license may be required if conducting auctions (IDFPR Auction License Act) - verify; pure brokerage via online platform partners may avoid [E].
